subject: ela
description: Students plan, draft, and revise informative or explanatory writing that examines a topic and conveys ideas, concepts, and information clearly. They introduce a topic, organize related ideas into logical groups, develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, and examples, use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary, link ideas with appropriate transitions, maintain a formal style, and provide a concluding statement that follows from the information presented. Because items are delivered in a self-contained format, every task embeds any source material, sentences, or student-draft excerpts the student needs to answer; students judge, organize, and improve informative writing rather than composing a full essay from nothing.
subSkills: Introduce a topic clearly and preview what is to follow
Organize ideas, concepts, and information into logical categories or groupings
Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, and examples
Distinguish relevant supporting evidence from irrelevant or off-topic content
Select precise language and domain-specific vocabulary appropriate to the topic
Use transitions to clarify relationships among ideas (for example, for instance, in addition, as a result, however)
Establish and maintain a formal, objective style and tone
Write a concluding statement or section that follows from and supports the information presented
Revise informative writing to improve clarity, organization, evidence, and word choice

problemArchetypes.name: Best topic-introduction sentence
problemArchetypes.example: A student is writing an informative article titled 'How Honeybees Make Honey.' Which opening sentence best introduces the topic for an informative text? Options offer a clear topic-and-preview sentence versus an opinion statement, a narrative hook, or an off-topic sentence.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify relevant vs. irrelevant detail
problemArchetypes.example: An informative paragraph about volcanoes is shown. The student must select the sentence that should be removed because it does not develop the topic with relevant facts (for example, a sentence stating the writer's favorite vacation spot).

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the correct transition
problemArchetypes.example: Two sentences are given: 'Most reptiles lay eggs. ___ some snakes give birth to live young.' The student selects the transition that signals the relationship (However) rather than one that signals addition or cause.

problemArchetypes.name: Logical organization / ordering
problemArchetypes.example: Four sentences from an informative paragraph are presented out of order. The student chooses the arrangement that introduces the topic, develops it with details, and closes logically.

problemArchetypes.name: Match evidence to a claim or topic sentence
problemArchetypes.example: A topic sentence about the benefits of recycling is shown with a short fact bank embedded in the item. The student selects the fact that best develops and supports the topic sentence.

problemArchetypes.name: Precise language and domain vocabulary
problemArchetypes.example: A draft sentence uses a vague word ('the thing that pushes blood'). The student selects the precise domain-specific term ('the heart') or the more accurate word choice that fits an informative, formal style.

problemArchetypes.name: Formal style and tone
problemArchetypes.example: An informative draft sentence is written casually ('Bats are super cool and kinda creepy'). The student selects the revision that maintains a formal, objective tone appropriate for informative writing.

problemArchetypes.name: Best concluding statement
problemArchetypes.example: A short informative passage about the water cycle is embedded in the item. The student selects the concluding sentence that follows from and summarizes the information presented, rather than one that introduces a new idea or states an opinion.

Easy.description: Single-sentence or two-sentence stimulus embedded in the item. The task is to identify or recognize a clear feature of informative writing (a topic sentence, an obvious irrelevant detail, a common transition, an obviously informal sentence). Answer is supported directly by the short stimulus with minimal inference.
constraints: Stimulus is one to two sentences, embedded in full in the item
Task verb is identify or recognize, not analyze or evaluate
Distinctions are clear-cut (for example, fact vs. personal opinion)
Familiar, concrete topics (animals, weather, everyday processes)
Domain vocabulary is common and previously taught

Medium.description: Short paragraph stimulus (3 to 5 sentences) embedded in the item. The student must analyze how parts work together: choose the best of several plausible details, order a few sentences, pick a transition where more than one is grammatically possible, or revise for precision or tone. Requires moderate inference about relevance and organization.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 5 sentence paragraph, embedded in full in the item
Task verb is analyze, organize, or revise
At least two answer choices are plausible and require comparison
Topic may be moderately unfamiliar academic content (ecosystems, simple history, how a system works)
Some distractors are relevant but weaker, not obviously wrong

Hard.description: Longer multi-paragraph or dense informative stimulus (6 to 10 sentences, possibly with a small embedded fact bank) in the item. The student must evaluate or synthesize: judge which evidence best develops a claim across the passage, choose a concluding statement that follows from the whole text, reorganize for the strongest logic, or revise a draft for both relevance and formal style at once. Requires sustained inference and weighing of close options.
constraints: Stimulus is 6 to 10 sentences or a short multi-paragraph excerpt, embedded in full in the item
Task verb is evaluate, synthesize, or judge the best of several strong options
Correct answer depends on information distributed across the stimulus, not one sentence
Topic is academic and may include unfamiliar domain vocabulary defined in context
Distractors are subtly flawed (relevant but redundant, accurate but off-topic, formal but unsupported)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses informative writing with opinion or persuasive writing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an opening or concluding sentence that states the writer's opinion or tries to persuade ('Everyone should protect bees') instead of one that objectively introduces or summarizes information

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks any sentence on the same general subject is relevant
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps or chooses a detail that mentions the topic word but does not actually develop the main idea (a personal anecdote or tangential fact)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats all transitions as interchangeable signals
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an addition transition (In addition) or a cause transition (As a result) where a contrast transition (However) is required by the relationship between ideas

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes a strong conclusion should add a new and interesting fact
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a concluding sentence that introduces brand-new information not supported by the passage instead of one that follows from what was presented

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student equates vivid, casual, or emotional language with good writing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a revision that is lively but informal or subjective ('Volcanoes are absolutely terrifying') over the precise, formal, objective choice

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student orders sentences by surface cues or first-mentioned rather than logical structure
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an arrangement that places a detail or conclusion before the topic is introduced, ignoring the introduce-develop-conclude structure

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the longest or most detailed evidence regardless of fit
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects the most elaborate fact even though it supports a different topic sentence than the one given

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student substitutes vague general words for precise domain vocabulary
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an imprecise phrase ('the thing in the sky that makes rain') over the accurate domain-specific term
